text: Time for the synthesis, putting all five principles together. We begin with the complete file, ContactForm.jsx. Here is the finished form. Every box takes what it shows from state, and every box reports its changes back to state. So this is source, components, ContactForm.jsx, and it opens by importing useState from React. Then inside the ContactForm function, lines four to eight hold five pieces of state, one for each part of the form. Name starts as an empty string. Topic starts as the string delivery. Message starts empty. WantsReply starts as false, and email starts as an empty string too. The note there is principle five. It starts with a string, never undefined. Next come the two handlers. handleMessageChange checks whether e.target.value.length is two hundred or less, and only then calls set Message with e.target.value. handleSend takes the event, calls e.preventDefault, and logs sent, followed by all five values. Then it puts every piece back. Set name to an empty string, set topic to delivery, set message to empty, set wantsReply to false, and set email to empty. Now the JSX, a section, a heading that says Contact Us, and a form whose on submit is handleSend. The name box gets value equals name in curly braces and an onChange that calls setName with e.target.value. That's principle three: value always comes with onChange. The topic menu works the same way with value equals topic on the select itself and three options inside it: delivery, payment, and other. Principle four: the choice lives on the select. The message text area gets value equals message, and its onChange is handleMessageChange. Principle two: state goes into the box. Right under it, a paragraph shows message.length out of two hundred. Then the tick box. It's an input of type checkbox with checked equals wantsReply, and its onChange calls setWantsReply with e.target.checked. Principle four again: the tick, not the text. Its label says, "Email me a reply." After that, wantsReply double ampersand and a label with the email box, so that box shows only when the tick is on. Its value is email, and its onChange calls setEmail with e.target.value. Principle one: every key goes into state. And at the very bottom, a button of type submit that says Send. The user fills in every part of the form, and that's what Figure Twenty-Six shows just before send. The name box says Anna. The topic menu is on payment. The message reads, "Where is my parcel?" And the count under it says nineteen out of two hundred. The box, Email me a reply, is ticked, so the email box is there holding anna@example.com. And below it all, the Send button. Then the user clicks Send. The console logs every value, and the whole form is back to its start. Look at Figure Twenty-Seven now. The name box is empty. The topic menu is back on delivery. The message is empty, and the count says zero out of two hundred. The tick box is clear, and down in the console, there's one line: Sent: Anna. Payment: Where is my parcel? True. anna@example.com. Logged from line eighteen of ContactForm.jsx. Notice the email box is gone too. Send saved false in wantsReply, so the double ampersand no longer shows it. Next, how React calls the components and what one key does. When the page loads, React starts at app and follows the tags. App has only one tag, so React calls ContactForm next. Figure Twenty-Eight draws that as a small tree. At the top, Main.jsx mounts app inside strict mode. Below it, step one is App, the root component. It's called first, and it returns the ContactForm tag. Under that, step two, ContactForm. It's called second, and it holds five states, one for each part of the form, and it's called again after every key, every pick, every tick, and every send. Every controlled box goes around the same loop on every key. Figure Twenty-Nine follows one key around that loop in four steps. One, the browser shows the new letter in the box just for a moment. Two, onChange, React calls our handler with the event object. Three, the setter, here set Message, saves the new text in state. And four, React renders again and writes the state back into the box through value, so the letter stays.
